The sharp noncommutative bilinear inequality

Written by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), Ultra, September 2026. New original text: public domain (CC0).

A finite domination coefficient is a starting budget. The preceding lesson produces such a budget for every bounded bilinear form. Here a curve through each input compares two vertical boundaries, and an exact finite phase average converts that comparison into a smaller budget. The operation is

C⟼C∥V∥.C\longmapsto\sqrt{C\|V\|}.C⟼C∥V∥​.

Its repeated application reaches coefficient one. A final compactness argument chooses four states that work simultaneously for every input.

We first construct the boundary curves and the scalar strip estimate, then explain how finite phases and affine state tests join them. Adjoining units and testing orthogonal isometries finish the arbitrary-algebra theorem and its optimality. No separability, nuclearity or trace assumption enters. Scalar order, continuous calculus, norm integrals and forced unitization are proved in CF1–10; the preceding lesson proves norm-preserving functional extension and arbitrary dual-ball compactness.

3. A scalar maximum bound and the strip estimate

Only locally convergent power series are needed for the scalar functions below. Their sums are continuous and complex differentiable by the same smaller-disk derivative estimate used above. Products are again locally convergent series: absolute convergence bounds the double sum, and regrouping by total degree gives its coefficients. A bounded bilinear form applied to two norm-convergent series has this property as well. Hence V(fx(z),fy(z))V(f_x(z),f_y(z))V(fx​(z),fy​(z)), and its products with scalar exponentials, belong to this class.

For the circle averages, use the scalar normalization proved in the preceding lesson's disk and quarter-phase construction. It gives eiπ/2=ie^{i\pi/2}=ieiπ/2=i; the exponential addition law therefore gives e2πi=1e^{2\pi i}=1e2πi=1. For a nonzero integer kkk, the primitive eikt/(ik)e^{ikt}/(ik)eikt/(ik) shows that its integral over [0,2π][0,2\pi][0,2π] is zero. The constant function has average one on that interval.

We prove the required maximum-modulus statement. Suppose h(z0+w)=∑m≥0γmwmh(z_0+w)=\sum_{m\ge0}\gamma_mw^mh(z0​+w)=∑m≥0​γm​wm on a disk. On a smaller circle of radius rrr, uniform absolute convergence permits multiplication and termwise Riemann integration. The elementary averages of ei(m−n)te^{i(m-n)t}ei(m−n)t are zero for m≠nm\ne nm=n and one for m=nm=nm=n. It follows that

12π∫02π∣h(z0+reit)∣2 dt=∑m≥0∣γm∣2r2m.\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|h(z_0+re^{it})|^2\,dt =\sum_{m\ge0}|\gamma_m|^2r^{2m}.2π1​∫02π​∣h(z0​+reit)∣2dt=m≥0∑​∣γm​∣2r2m.

If ∣h∣|h|∣h∣ has a local maximum at z0z_0z0​, the left side is at most ∣γ0∣2|\gamma_0|^2∣γ0​∣2. Every other term is nonnegative, so γm=0\gamma_m=0γm​=0 for m≥1m\ge1m≥1; hhh is constant near z0z_0z0​.

Now let hhh be continuous on a closed rectangle and locally represented by power series in its interior. Its modulus attains a maximum by compactness of the rectangle, proved in CF1. If the maximum exceeded every boundary value, it would occur inside. The set of interior points attaining that maximum is relatively closed and, by the circle argument, relatively open. It is the whole interior. To see this explicitly, parameterize a segment from a point in that set to any other interior point. The parameters belonging to the set form a relatively open and closed subset of [0,1][0,1][0,1] containing zero. The supremum of the parameters up to which the entire initial interval is included belongs to the set by closedness; if it were less than one, openness would extend that interval past the supremum. Thus the segment is entirely included. Thus the modulus is constant throughout the interior, and continuity gives that same value on the boundary, a contradiction. The modulus on the rectangle is therefore bounded by its boundary maximum. This proves precisely the maximum bound we shall use.

Here the state tests concern the nonzero algebras of Theorem 1.1. For unital algebras, a positive element ppp has a state attaining ∥p∥\|p\|∥p∥: evaluation at its largest spectral value on C∗(1,p)C^*(1,p)C∗(1,p) extends with unchanged norm and value one at the unit. Such an extension is positive. To check the last assertion, if ∥f∥=f(1)=1\|f\|=f(1)=1∥f∥=f(1)=1, the first-order expansion of f(eith)f(e^{ith})f(eith) for self-adjoint hhh, and its modulus bound for both signs of ttt, force f(h)f(h)f(h) to be real. For 0≤h≤10\le h\le10≤h≤1, ∣1−f(h)∣≤∥1−h∥≤1|1-f(h)|\le\|1-h\|\le1∣1−f(h)∣≤∥1−h∥≤1 then gives f(h)≥0f(h)\ge0f(h)≥0; scaling handles every positive element. This uses the functional extension and scalar calculus already proved in the preceding lesson and CF1–10.

The state set is a nonempty weak-star compact convex set. Indeed it is the intersection of the compact dual unit ball with the closed conditions of positivity and value one at the unit. The full arbitrary dual-ball construction is in Sections 9.1–9.5 of the preceding lesson.

9. Exercises through the four mechanisms

State selection and the endpoint

Exercise 1. Given finite families in unital A,BA,BA,B, choose normers for their four positive square sums. Explain why the converse of Lemma 1.2 needs those four choices, and why averaging within an algebra too early can lose the family cost RRR. Test a common normer on x=e12∈M2x=e_{12}\in M_2x=e12​∈M2​.

Solution. Write

Sx=∑jxj∗xj,Tx=∑jxjxj∗,Sy=∑jyj∗yj,Ty=∑jyjyj∗.S_x=\sum_jx_j^*x_j,\quad T_x=\sum_jx_jx_j^*,\qquad S_y=\sum_jy_j^*y_j,\quad T_y=\sum_jy_jy_j^*.Sx​=j∑​xj∗​xj​,Tx​=j∑​xj​xj∗​,Sy​=j∑​yj∗​yj​,Ty​=j∑​yj​yj∗​.

Each positive element has a state attaining its norm by the scalar detector construction in Section 5. Assign its four independent normers to φ1,φ2,ψ1,ψ2\varphi_1,\varphi_2,\psi_1,\psi_2φ1​,φ2​,ψ1​,ψ2​, in that order. Then the sums of the two family brackets are exactly

φ1(Sx)+φ2(Tx)=R(x),ψ1(Sy)+ψ2(Ty)=R(y).\varphi_1(S_x)+\varphi_2(T_x)=R(x),\qquad \psi_1(S_y)+\psi_2(T_y)=R(y).φ1​(Sx​)+φ2​(Tx​)=R(x),ψ1​(Sy​)+ψ2​(Ty​)=R(y).

The finite weighted affine test consequently has the maximum needed in the converse proof.

Within M2M_2M2​, x=e12x=e_{12}x=e12​ gives Sx=e22S_x=e_{22}Sx​=e22​ and Tx=e11T_x=e_{11}Tx​=e11​. Both have norm one, but a state taking value one on both would take value two on e11+e22=1e_{11}+e_{22}=1e11​+e22​=1, whereas a state has value one there. Thus a common normer can fail in either algebra. Replacing the two separate normers by their mean before evaluating the two sums need not give the sum of their norms. Four choices preserve the exact two equalities above.

Exercise 8. For the improvement operation on nonzero unital algebras, treat V=0V=0V=0 and V≠0V\ne0V=0 separately. In the latter case prove C≥∥V∥/2C\ge\|V\|/2C≥∥V∥/2 for every admissible coefficient, attain its infimum by compactness, and justify the division in the best-constant argument. Explain how iteration reaches the same endpoint.

Solution. If V=0V=0V=0, every input has bilinear value zero, and any quadruple of states works. The nonzero algebras have states by the unit-value extension construction, so none needs to be manufactured by dividing a zero quantity.

Exact finite phase bookkeeping

Exercise 2. Expand (X∗X)2(X^*X)^2(X∗X)2 without commuting its coefficients. Identify the two surviving pairings of indices and their intersection, and obtain the exact all-equal subtraction in (6). Check the formula for a single coefficient.

Solution. The term indexed by i,j,k,li,j,k,li,j,k,l is ζi‾ζjζk‾ζlxi∗xjxk∗xl\overline{\zeta_i}\zeta_j\overline{\zeta_k}\zeta_l x_i^*x_jx_k^*x_lζi​​ζj​ζk​​ζl​xi∗​xj​xk∗​xl​. Its expectation survives exactly when {i,k}={j,l}\{i,k\}=\{j,l\}{i,k}={j,l} as multisets. The pattern i=j,k=li=j,k=li=j,k=l sums to (∑ixi∗xi)2=S2(\sum_i x_i^*x_i)^2=S^2(∑i​xi∗​xi​)2=S2. The pattern i=l,j=ki=l,j=ki=l,j=k, in the displayed multiplication order, sums to ∑ixi∗Txi\sum_i x_i^*T x_i∑i​xi∗​Txi​. Their intersection forces all four indices to be equal and contributes ∑i(xi∗xi)2\sum_i(x_i^*x_i)^2∑i​(xi∗​xi​)2. Inclusion–exclusion gives

E(X∗X)2=S2+∑ixi∗Txi−∑i(xi∗xi)2.\mathbb E(X^*X)^2 =S^2+\sum_i x_i^*T x_i-\sum_i(x_i^*x_i)^2.E(X∗X)2=S2+i∑​xi∗​Txi​−i∑​(xi∗​xi​)2.

Every valid pattern outside the intersection was counted once, and each intersection term is now counted once. For one coefficient the first two terms are both (x∗x)2(x^*x)^2(x∗x)2, so subtracting the third leaves exactly the required single copy.

Exercise 3. Replace continuous independent phases in the fourth-moment calculation by a finite distribution. Show that independent uniform third roots give the same surviving monomials, count the sample points, and decide whether roots of other orders or real signs work. State what this calculation establishes about interpolation.

Solution. For ω3=1\omega^3=1ω3=1, ω≠1\omega\ne1ω=1, the average over its three roots is

Eζk=(1+ωk+ω2k)/3=0(k=−2,−1,1,2),Eζ0=1.\mathbb E\zeta^k=(1+\omega^k+\omega^{2k})/3 =0\quad(k=-2,-1,1,2),\qquad \mathbb E\zeta^0=1.Eζk=(1+ωk+ω2k)/3=0(k=−2,−1,1,2),Eζ0=1.

A fourth-moment monomial has only exponents from −2-2−2 to 222 in each coordinate. The product average factors into the coordinate averages and is nonzero exactly when every exponent is zero. Continuous uniform phases have the same criterion by the elementary integral of integer powers around the circle. Thus the pairings and exact fourth moments coincide.

The independent three-root product has exactly 3n3^n3n equally weighted points. It is an exact formula, not an approximation by sampled phases. Uniform roots of any order m≥3m\ge3m≥3 also have zero average for those four nonzero exponents and give the same result. Signs have nonzero second-power average and retain extra monomials. The finite distribution establishes the moment and diagonal-extraction identities; the strip estimate still needs its separate analytic proof.

Solution. With conjugated phases, expansion and finite summation give

EV(X,Y)=∑i,jE[ζiζj‾] V(xi,yj).\mathbb E V(X,Y) =\sum_{i,j}\mathbb E[\zeta_i\overline{\zeta_j}]\,V(x_i,y_j).EV(X,Y)=i,j∑​E[ζi​ζj​​]V(xi​,yj​).

The diagonal coefficient is E∣ζi∣2=1\mathbb E|\zeta_i|^2=1E∣ζi​∣2=1. For i≠ji\ne ji=j, independence and the zero means give coefficient zero. Every diagonal term is therefore retained and (12) follows.

For the same phases in both inputs, the coefficient is E[ζiζj]\mathbb E[\zeta_i\zeta_j]E[ζi​ζj​]. It vanishes off the diagonal by independence and on the diagonal by Eζi2=0\mathbb E\zeta_i^2=0Eζi2​=0. That choice makes the entire average zero, even when the intended sum of diagonal bilinear values is nonzero. Conjugation is determined by the bilinear convention.

Unitization and the two bidual variables

Exercise 9. Prove the exact norm identity (14), including its value on the canonical copies of A,BA,BA,B. Verify that composition with the contractive canonical unitization maps preserves that norm. Independently construct a norm-preserving unitized extension from two-sided positive approximate identities and compactness of the projective-tensor dual ball.

Solution. The definition of TTT gives

∥T∥=sup⁡∥x∥,∥y∥≤1∣(Tx)(y)∣=∥V∥.\|T\|=\sup_{\|x\|,\|y\|\le1}|(Tx)(y)|=\|V\|.∥T∥=∥x∥,∥y∥≤1sup​∣(Tx)(y)∣=∥V∥.

For F∈A∗∗,G∈B∗∗F\in A^{**},G\in B^{**}F∈A∗∗,G∈B∗∗, the dual norm estimates yield

∣F(T∗G)∣≤∥F∥∥T∗G∥≤∥V∥∥F∥∥G∥.|F(T^*G)|\le\|F\|\|T^*G\| \le\|V\|\|F\|\|G\|.∣F(T∗G)∣≤∥F∥∥T∗G∥≤∥V∥∥F∥∥G∥.

Evaluation embeddings are isometric by norming functionals, and

(T∗JBy)(x)=(JBy)(Tx)=V(x,y),V‾(JAx,JBy)=V(x,y).(T^*J_By)(x)=(J_By)(Tx)=V(x,y),\qquad \overline V(J_Ax,J_By)=V(x,y).(T∗JB​y)(x)=(JB​y)(Tx)=V(x,y),V(JA​x,JB​y)=V(x,y).

The upper norm bound and this restriction prove ∥V‾∥=∥V∥\|\overline V\|=\|V\|∥V∥=∥V∥. Under the canonical C*-bidual construction, the maps a+λ1↦JAa+λ1A∗∗a+\lambda1\mapsto J_Aa+\lambda1_{A^{**}}a+λ1↦JA​a+λ1A∗∗​ are unital *-homomorphisms, hence contractive by CF6. Composition cannot increase the upper bound, while its restriction still gives VVV, so this particular unitized form also has norm exactly ∥V∥\|V\|∥V∥. These calculations do not assert separate normality in both variables.

For the direct construction, use the finite-set contractions

e=HF(HF+δ1)−1,HF=∑a∈F(a∗a+aa∗).e=H_F(H_F+\delta1)^{-1},\qquad H_F=\sum_{a\in F}(a^*a+aa^*).e=HF​(HF​+δ1)−1,HF​=a∈F∑​(a∗a+aa∗).

They belong to AAA, are positive with norm at most one, and for a∈Fa\in Fa∈F

∥a−ae∥2, ∥a−ea∥2≤∥(1−e)HF(1−e)∥≤sup⁡t≥0δ2t(t+δ)2=δ/4.\|a-ae\|^2,\ \|a-ea\|^2 \le\|(1-e)H_F(1-e)\| \le\sup_{t\ge0}\frac{\delta^2t}{(t+\delta)^2} =\delta/4.∥a−ae∥2, ∥a−ea∥2≤∥(1−e)HF​(1−e)∥≤t≥0sup​(t+δ)2δ2t​=δ/4.

The two inequalities use a∗aa^*aa∗a and aa∗aa^*aa∗, respectively; the C*-identity can be applied to z∗zz^*zz∗z or zz∗zz^*zz∗. Increasing the finite set and decreasing δ\deltaδ gives approximation on both sides for every element. The corresponding contractions fff do the same in BBB.

The unitized forms We,f(s,t)=V(se,tf)W_{e,f}(s,t)=V(se,tf)We,f​(s,t)=V(se,tf) have norm at most ∥V∥\|V\|∥V∥ and converge to VVV on original inputs. Each defines a functional on A†⊗^πB†A^\dagger\widehat\otimes_\pi B^\daggerA†⊗​π​B† with the same norm: bound its value on every finite decomposition by the projective cost, extend by completeness, and use elementary tensors for the reverse inequality. The preceding lesson's compact dual-ball proof supplies a convergent subnet of these functionals. Its limit gives one bounded bilinear form on both unitizations, with upper norm bound ∥V∥\|V\|∥V∥, whose original restriction is VVV. That restriction forces the lower bound. Thus this construction also preserves the norm, including when V=0V=0V=0, and supplies the extension used in the main nonunital proof.

References

Gilles Pisier, Grothendieck's Theorem, past and present, expanded UNCUT author version, 21 August 2013, Theorem 7.1 and (7.1)–(7.3), printed p.25 (PDF p.27), gives the four-state and finite-family formulations and their normalizations. The sharp theorem there is attributed to Haagerup. Section 11, printed pp.35–36 (PDF pp.37–38), proves the finite CAR optimality construction for the maximum-of-two-norms normalization. The orthogonal-isometry test in Section 8 here proves optimality for the four-state coefficient directly.

Gilles Pisier, Grothendieck inequality, random matrices and quantum expanders, Kyoto lectures recorded by Kei Hasegawa, March 2015, §5, pp.9–10, presents the phase fourth-moment and three-lines improvement used in Sections 4 and 6. Remark 5.3 credits these steps to Pisier's 1978 work and the finiteness ingredient to Haagerup. The lecture's subsequent finiteness step is an outline; here the finite starting bound comes from the preceding two lessons, and Sections 2–3 and 7 supply the norm-series, scalar strip and nonunital arguments.

The random-lift lesson and the completion and state-domination lesson provide the finite starting constant and full affine compactness argument. The scalar and C*-foundations are CF1–10. The canonical bidual notation uses the universal all-state/predual construction followed by the concrete support and polar-decomposition proof. The strip, norm-series and direct unitization arguments are given in full above.
